claim: Overburden, pore-pressure and fracture gradients are the pressures divided by true vertical depth from the derrick floor, so every gradient falls as the air gap rises.
quote: Overburden gradient (O), pressure gradient (P), and fracture gradient (F) are defined as the respective pressures divided by the true vertical depth referenced to the derrick floor, i.e. referenced to the top of the mud column. All the gradients decrease as the rig floor elevation increases i.e. as the air gap increases.
In this report gradients are expressed in pounds per gallon (ppg) where 1 psi/ft = 19.25 ppg = 2.31 g/cc.

claim: Overburden gradient O = [8.5 W + rho_avg (D - W - A)]/D with sea water at 8.5 ppg.
quote: The overburden gradient is related to height of the water column and the sediment column by the equation: O =[(8.5)(W) + (rho avg)(D-W-A)]/D

claim: Average sediment density in ppg: rho_avg = 16.3 + {(D-W-A)/3125}^0.6; with W 2,000 ft and A 50 ft this gives O = 13.7 ppg at 5,200 ft and 16.7 ppg at 12,300 ft.
quote: As an example, if W and A are 2000 feet and 50 feet, respectively, the overburden gradient is 13.7 ppg if D is 5200 feet and 16.7 ppg if D is 12300 feet.

claim: A textbook 1 psi/ft overburden is not recommended in deepwater.
quote: Use of a text book value of 1 psi/ft (19.25 ppg) as an estimate for the overburden gradient is also not recommended for deepwater interpretations.

claim: Fracture pressure is taken equal to the minimum horizontal stress; k = (F-P)/(O-P) and F = k(O-P) + P.
quote: Fracture pressure is assumed equal to the minimum horizontal stress. The ratio of minimum horizontal effective stress to vertical effective stress (k) is defined as follows: k = (F-P) / (O-P)

claim: Empirical stress ratio k = 0.039 (D - W/4 - A)^0.33, constants fitted by the author to Gulf of Mexico leak-off tests; k rises with depth below the mudline.
quote: where the constants in the empirical method have been derived by the author from leak off test (LOT) data from the Gulf of Mexico.

claim: Seven estimates of k: empirical, uniaxial strain nu/(1-nu), plastic k = 1, solidity 1 - phi, hoop stress 2nu/(1-nu), failure 1/[(mu^2+1)^0.5 + mu]^2, fault angle 1/tan^2(theta).
quote: Stress ratio, k, has been estimated using several approaches as listed below

claim: Example: P = 8.5 ppg, D = 5,200 ft, O = 13.4 ppg, k = 0.63 gives F = 11.6 ppg.
quote: If pore pressure is normal (i.e. P is 8.5 ppg) and D and O are 5200 feet and 13.4 ppg respectively from the last example, fracture gradient is 11.6 ppg, assuming a k of 0.63 from the empirical approach.
An example is the classical equivalent depth relationship: P = O - (Oe-8.5)(De/D)

claim: Horizontal (Eaton) model: P = O - (O - 8.5)(M/E)^x with x = 3 for velocity or travel time and 1.2 for resistivity.
quote: The horizontal derived pressure in Figure 2 is 14.1 ppg assuming a value of 3 for the exponent. (Use 1.2 for resistivity data.)

claim: Default porosity-depth trend phi = 0.41 - (D-W-A)/45,455, floor 0.025 below 17,500 ft of sediment, intercept adjusted to data.
quote: where phi is fractional porosity and the constant, 0.41, is adjusted to fit available data. If (D-W-A) is > 17,500 feet, set phi equal to 0.025.

claim: The normal pressure gradient is itself uncertain and can be as high as 8.95 ppg.
quote: Another uncertainty in both models is the normal pressure gradient; it can be as hight as 8.95 ppg.

claim: Above the centroid the shale pressure is about 50 psi lower than the adjacent reservoir per 100 ft; reservoir pressure at a crest can equal the fracture pressure of the overlying shale.
quote: The net effect is that the pressure in shales is about 50 psi lower than the pressure in the juxtaposed reservoir for each 100 feet above the centroid. The effect is larger if hydrocarbons are present because of buoyancy.

claim: Recommends vertical models use the mean effective stress (O-P)(1+2k)/3; because k increases with depth the predicted pressures rise.
quote: Modify vertical prediction models as a function of the orthogonal mean effective stress instead of vertical effective stress, i.e. (O-P)(1+2k)/3 instead of (O-P). Because k tends to increase with depth, the resultant pore pressure predictions will be higher using mean stress values (and more aligned with measurements?).
